At Reuters Events Pharma and other events in the past days, I kept hearing the same question: “How can we use AI to be more efficient?” But that lens feels too limited. Take Klarna as an example ( https://lnkd.in/ejnyHGxE ). They rolled out an AI assistant to handle customer service—effectively taking on the workload of around 700 agents. The headline takeaway is cost savings. But that’s not the most interesting part. What’s really happening is a complete rethink of how customer interactions are designed in the first place. It’s not just optimization—it’s a shift to a different operating model. In pharma, most AI efforts in comercial today are still focused on: - speeding up content creation - improving targeting - reducing manual work All useful—but largely incremental. The bigger question we should be asking is: 👉 If AI takes on a significant share of today’s work, how should our roles actually evolve? Not “how do we do the same things faster?” But “what should exist now that didn’t before?” ...more

This year I finally stopped lying to myself. For years I told myself I was “too busy” to do something I always desired to do: to walk the Camino de Santiago. The truth? I wasn’t too busy. It just never became important enough. So this year, I made it important. I took a real break and walked the Camino. Yesterday, I arrived in Santiago de Compostela. After eight long days of walking, three things stayed with me. Not only about the Camino, but about how we think about life, work, time and progress. 1. Distance doesn’t care how tired you are. Some days were simply long. No dramatic moments. No breathtaking scenery. Just kilometer after kilometer with sore feet, wondering why the finish never seemed any closer. Thinking about how much was left only made it harder. Focusing on the next few steps made it manageable. The same happens with long projects, difficult quarters, or challenging periods in life. The distance doesn’t shrink because you’re exhausted. Your focus is the only variable you actually control. 2. Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. Eight days of walking for something a train does in eight hours. On paper, a terrible trade. But the Camino was never about reaching Santiago faster. The eight days were the point. Yet we spend so much of our lives optimizing for speed: how much we earn, how quickly we get promoted, how we compare ourselves to the person next to us. Often we’re measuring ourselves with someone else’s ruler. Maybe it’s worth asking who set the pace we’re trying so hard to keep up with—and whether it’s actually ours. 3. The destination stays still. You don’t. There isn’t one Camino. There are many: Francés, Portugués, del Norte, Primitivo. Different starting points, different landscapes, different people. They all end in the same square in Santiago. Many people come back and walk it again, choosing a different route every time. Same destination. Completely different journey. Because the road changes. And so do you, every time you walk it. The destination stays still. You don’t. None of these ideas are new. Focus on the next step. Define success on your own terms. Remember the journey matters more than the destination. We’ve all heard them a hundred times. So why do we know them so well, and apply them so rarely? #CaminoDeSantiago #Leadership #Reflection #4Zones

This was one of the best panels I have attended for a while. Iria Gala from Novo Nordisk , Necati Sebe from GSK and Angela Duffy from Astellas Pharma were expertly navigated by the moderator, Sabine Louët across a wide-ranging discussion. Their lived experience of harnessing the potential of AI within their organisations was both thought-provoking and inspiring. Top 10 takeaways - my favourites are 9 and 10: 1️⃣ The shift from AI as a productivity tool to AI as a source of business transformation is underway. It affects every aspect of an organisation, from talent and organisation design to end-to-end workflow redesign. We all need to get comfortable with feeling uncomfortable with this pace. 2️⃣ Organisations know mindsets need to shift but many lack a structured way to do this. Breaking silos requires cultural change, not just AI: the data exists, but the cross-functional conversation does not. 3️⃣ Change management is critical. According to change management consultants Prosci , it delivers 7x more impact than tech tools alone. Identifying "micro-moments" in people's days, and showing how AI can improve them, accelerates adoption, e.g. in coaching discussions during field sales meetings. 4️⃣ Being transparent about uncertainty is critical to maintain trust and credibility. 5️⃣ It's too early to prove ROI. But life science companies already invest large amounts in other areas where ROI is hard to demonstrate e.g. congresses. Historically, life sciences has accepted that only 1-2% of drug innovations will succeed but continued to invest. A similar mindset is needed for AI innovations. 6️⃣ Life sciences need to look to other sectors, such as finance, for inspiration and insight on what may deliver a meaningful return. 7️⃣ Risk tolerance needs to be recalibrated. Different types of activities need to be categorised against commensurate levels of risk. 8️⃣ 80+% of doctors already use AI in daily life; field reps are doing the same, as are patients. Processes and ways of working need to adapt to this reality. Unsanctioned use of AI tools is a key risk to businesses, so leaders have an obligation to provide fit-for-purpose tools before employees find workarounds. 9️⃣ The global vs local relationship needs to be refined. Global sets direction and selects enterprise-wide platforms. Local markets get autonomy within governance guardrails to execute and pilot, and pilots close to the customer and operation have a higher success rate. 🔟 Field reps will evolve into insight agents, not just message deliverers, working with AI as partners. What can life sciences learn from financial services? What does the focus on local relationships and deployment means for the recent centralisation at regional level that's taken place in many life science companies? #PharmaAI #DigitalHealth #PharmaCommercial #ChangeManagement #LifeSciences #AIAdoption

¿Y si el problema nunca fue tu talento... sino el lugar donde intentabas demostrarlo? Hay momentos de la vida en los que empiezas a dudar de ti. Porque un proyecto no sale como esperabas. Porque alguien deja de confiar en ti. Porque sientes que, hagas lo que hagas, no terminas de encajar. Y es fácil pensar: "Quizá no valgo tanto como pensaba." Sin embargo, la historia de los tres entrenadores que llevaron a la Selección Española a lo más alto demuestra que, antes de tocar la cima del éxito, también fueron cuestionados, rechazados y señalados por sus resultados: Luis Aragonés se marchó del Betis por sus desavenencias con el presidente. Vicente del Bosque salió del Real Madrid y su siguiente aventura en Turquía apenas duró unos meses. Luis de la Fuente fue destituido del Deportivo Alavés tras solo nueve partidos oficiales. Si hubiéramos juzgado sus carreras en esos momentos, muchos habrían llegado a la misma conclusión: "Ya no tienen nada más que aportar." Pero, por suerte, la historia no había terminado para ellos. Luis Aragonés conquistó la Eurocopa con 69 años. Vicente del Bosque levantó el Mundial con 59. Luis de la Fuente ha ganado la Eurocopa con 63 y el Mundial con 65 años. Entonces, ¿qué fue lo que cambió? No cambió su capacidad, sino el lugar donde pudieron demostrar todo su valor. No encajar en un lugar no significa que no tengas la capacidad necesaria. Un mal resultado no define toda una trayectoria. Y que alguien no vea tu potencial no significa que ese potencial no exista. Además, hay otro detalle que solemos pasar por alto: la edad. Vivimos obsesionados con llegar pronto, cuando muchas veces la experiencia, la serenidad y la capacidad para liderar se construyen con los años. Porque una carrera profesional no es una fotografía. Es una película. Y, a veces, el mejor capítulo llega cuando menos lo esperas.
activity.text_en: What if the problem was never your talent… but the place where you were trying to prove it? There are moments in life when you start to doubt yourself. Because a project doesn't go as expected. Because someone stops trusting you. Because you feel that, whatever you do, you don't quite fit in. And it's easy to think, “Maybe I'm not worth as much as I thought I was." However, the story of the three coaches who led the Spanish National Team to the top shows that, before reaching the peak of success, they were also questioned, rejected and singled out for their results: Luis Aragonés left Betis because of his disagreements with the president. Vicente del Bosque left Real Madrid and his next adventure in Turkey lasted just a few months. Luis de la Fuente was sacked from Deportivo Alavés after only nine official matches. If we had judged their careers at the time, many would have come to the same conclusion: “They have nothing more to contribute.“ But luckily, the story wasn't over for them. Luis Aragonés won the European Championship at the age of 69. Vicente del Bosque lifted the World Cup with 59. Luis de la Fuente has won the Euro at 63 and the World Cup at 65. So what changed? It didn't change their ability, but the place where they were able to prove their worth. Not fitting in doesn't mean you don't have the capacity. A bad result does not define an entire trajectory. And just because someone doesn't see your potential doesn't mean that potential doesn't exist. In addition, there is another detail that we tend to overlook: age. We live obsessed with arriving early, when many times experience, serenity and the ability to lead are built over the years. Because a professional career is not a photograph. It's a movie. And sometimes the best chapter comes when you least expect it.

IKEA used AI to replace 8,500 customer service roles. Then did something most companies wouldn't. They retrained the people. Instead of removing jobs, they moved employees into interior design advisory roles. The result? A new service line that reportedly generated $1.4 billion in revenue. That's the part worth paying attention to. AI is very good at repetitive work. Humans are still better at judgment. Relationships. Taste. Trust. The companies that win with AI won't be the ones that automate everything. They'll be the ones that automate the right things. And then move their people closer to where they create the most value. That's a much more interesting future than humans versus AI. It's humans with AI. How is your company thinking about AI: cost reduction or value creation? Last week, someone asked me what I enjoy most about moderating a panel. They assumed the answer would be standing on stage. It isn't. The people on the stage are not the most important people in the room. The audience is. Before every keynote or panel discussion, I ask myself two questions. Where is the audience today? Where does the organiser want them to be by the end of the session? Everything I do starts there. If I'm moderating, my role is to help the speakers relax so they can be themselves. The best conversations happen when people stop worrying about saying the "right" thing and simply share what they've learned. If I'm delivering a keynote, I don't start by asking, "What do I want to say?" I start by asking, "What does the audience need to hear?" Then I look for stories, experiences and examples that help them see a familiar challenge from a different perspective. Because information alone rarely changes behaviour. People change when something shifts the way they think and feel. If someone leaves the room with one new perspective they can put into practice tomorrow, then we've achieved something worthwhile. Thank you, Gaurav, for your generous feedback. Reading your reflections reminded me why I still love stepping onto a stage. What about you? Whether you're speaking, leading a meeting or presenting to your team, do you start with what you want to say, or with what your audience needs to hear? #Cheemia #Pharma #DigitalTransformation #LifeSciences
